title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup

epigraph.quote: Never argue with the tape. A great fundamental story in a Stage 3 downtrend is a falling knife until institutional accumulation builds a floor and reclaims the key moving averages.
epigraph.author: Stan Weinstein (paraphrased from Secrets for Profiting in Bull and Bear Markets)

web_blocks.html: While ASE Technology's Q3 2026 fundamentals and October 2026 monthly revenue (+47% YoY) are strong, the price tape on November 13, 2026 is weak [14, 16]. ASX closed at $35.55 (-2.04% 1D, +12.39% 1W, -15.13% 1M on the 21-day facts ledger; -22.55% rolling 30D on TradingView), sitting -25.8% below its $47.93 52-week high [14, 16, 22]. On the facts ledger, ASX is classified as Stage 3 (Topping / Pullback) above its 200-day SMA ($34.14), while our technical screen flags CAP_REJECTED / AVOID_STAGE4_OR_BROKEN because price sits -13.61% below its 50-day SMA ($41.15), -6.91% below its 30-week SMA ($38.19), and -7.54% below its 10-week EMA ($38.45) [14, 22].

Multi-timeframe inspection across Weekly (1W), Daily (1D), and 4-Hour (4H) charts reveals a Dislocation at Major Shelf setup without a confirmed turn [21]. ASX sits near Pivot S1 ($35.21) and +4.13% above its rising 200-day SMA ($34.14), with its 20-day swing low at $29.58 and Pivot S2 at $30.91 [14, 21, 22]. However, the 4-hour trend remains downward: close ($35.55) sits beneath the 4H 20-EMA ($36.41) and 4H 50-SMA ($39.25), while Daily RSI14 is 43.36 (4H RSI 44.89; 1W RSI 48.20) [21, 22]. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 is in a Correction regime (below 50-DMA, 6 distribution days, 52.6% breadth above 50-DMA), creating headwinds for a 2.92-beta ADR [22].

web_blocks.takeaway: ASX is testing the confluence of Pivot S1 ($35.21) and its 200-day SMA ($34.14), but neither the 4-hour chart nor the weekly moving averages have turned up. Short-term trading momentum is negative.

web_blocks.html: From an institutional flow and options-desk perspective, two details stand out. First, short interest is negligible at 0.50% of float (11.03 million shares, 1.37 days to cover), meaning the -22.55% selloff was driven by institutional profit-taking and macro de-risking rather than an aggressive short attack [13]. Second, our deterministic options scan (options_snapshot.py) stamps NO_OPTIONS_EDGE: the $35/$37.50 bull call spread costs $1.13 for a maximum gain of $1.37, yielding a 1.21:1 reward-to-risk ratio that fails our 1.25:1 minimum hurdle [21]. Without a confirmed 4H turn or cheap call-spread convexity, both short-term traders and options buyers should stand aside.

book_paragraphs: If Chapter 7 showed us that ASE Technology's valuation is reasonable on forward earnings, Chapter 8 delivers the cold shower of market reality: right now, the chart is broken. As of the November 13, 2026 close at $35.55, ASX is in a Weinstein Stage 3 topping/pullback phase on the daily ledger, sitting 13.6% below its 50-day moving average and nearly 7% below its 30-week moving average.

Notice the disconnect that trips up so many fundamental investors. On October 29, ASE delivered a blowout Q3 print—revenue up 44.8%, ATM gross margins at 30.6%, and LEAP guidance hiked above $4 billion. Two weeks later, October monthly revenue came in up 47% year-over-year. Yet the stock is down 22.5% in a month from its $47.93 high. Why? Because the stock had already tripled off its $13.35 52-week low, and in a broader US market correction with six distribution days on the S&P 500, institutions used the liquidity of a great earnings print to lock in gains.

When you inspect the tape across Weekly, Daily, and 4-Hour timeframes, you see a classic 'dislocation at a major shelf.' ASX bounced 9.7% off its Pivot S1 support at $35.21 this past week, and it sits just 4.1% above its rising 200-day simple moving average at $34.14. That 200-day line is the line in the sand for long-term institutional sponsorship.

Should a short-term momentum trader jump in right here? No. Look at the 4-hour chart: the stock is still trapped beneath its 4-hour 20-EMA at $36.41, and RSI sits in the low-to-mid 40s across every timeframe—48.2 weekly, 43.4 daily, 44.9 four-hour. There is no confirmed turn yet. Even in the options market, implied volatility has priced out the easy upside: a $35/$37.50 call spread costs $1.13 for $1.37 of max profit—just 1.21-to-1, below our desk's 1.25-to-1 minimum.

And notice what is NOT happening: short sellers are not piling on. Short interest is a tiny 0.50% of float. This is long-only profit-taking and high-beta (2.92 beta) risk reduction. For disciplined capital, that means patience: wait for the $33.25–$35.75 support shelf to hold and for price to reclaim at least the 4-hour 20-EMA ($36.41) and 10-week EMA ($38.45) on expanding volume before treating ASX as an active momentum trade again.

Let's walk through the exact price map so there is zero ambiguity when you look at your TradingView screen on Monday morning. Above today's $35.55 close sits a dense ceiling of overhead supply: first the 4-hour 20-EMA at $36.41, then the 30-week SMA at $38.19, the 20-day SMA at $38.35, and the 10-week EMA at $38.45. Above that cluster sits the 50-day SMA at $41.15—13.61% above Friday's close—and Classic Pivot R1 at $45.86, which aligns almost to the penny with our $44.50–$46.00 base-case resistance zone.

Below today's close, the market has carved out two clear lines of defense. The first is the immediate shelf between Pivot S1 ($35.21) and the rising 200-day SMA ($34.14). That is why our support buy zone spans $33.25 to $35.75: it gives the stock room to test and slightly undercut the 200-day moving average intraday without triggering a false stop. The second line is Pivot S2 at $30.91—which also happens to sit right next to your Schwab cost basis of $30.50 per share. Our hard invalidation stop at $31.75 is placed deliberately between the 200-day SMA ($34.14) and S2 ($30.91), using roughly 1.3x the 14-day Average True Range ($2.83) so normal daily volatility does not shake you out prematurely, while ensuring you never ride a broken Stage 3 trend back down into the $20s.

Finally, let's check the broader market tape because no high-beta ADR trades in a vacuum. As of November 13, 2026, the S&P 500 is in an official Correction regime—below its 50-day moving average, above its 200-day moving average, with six institutional distribution days over the last 25 sessions and only 52.6% of index constituents holding above their 50-day lines. With ASX carrying a 2.92 one-year beta, every 1% market wobble tends to translate into a 2.5% to 3% swing in ASX. Respecting that volatility is why we keep new cash sidelined until the 4-hour and weekly charts prove buyers have regained control.

book_subsections.title: Anatomy of the October–November 2026 Stage 3 Pullback
paragraphs: To understand why ASX fell 22.55% in a single month despite beating Q3 earnings and posting +47% YoY October revenue, you have to look at the preceding twelve months. From its 52-week low of $13.35, ASX surged more than 250% to hit $47.93 in October 2026. By the time Q3 results were released on October 29, the stock was wildly extended above its 30-week and 200-day moving averages. In technical analysis, when a high-beta leader (2.92 beta) is stretched far above its long-term trendlines and the broader S&P 500 enters a Correction with six distribution days, even a stellar earnings beat becomes a 'sell the news' liquidity event for fast-money funds.

That selling pressure pushed ASX cleanly below its 20-day SMA ($38.35), its 30-week SMA ($38.19), its 10-week EMA ($38.45), and its 50-day SMA ($41.15), officially flipping our scanner to Stage 3 (CAP_REJECTED) (CAP_REJECTED). Crucially, however, volume on the recent bounce has been orderly—average daily volume is 8.04 million shares with a 0.96x relative volume ratio—and short interest remains tiny at 0.50% of float. This is not a structural fraud or solvency panic; it is a classic valuation and positioning reset.

book_subsections.title: What Must Happen for a Stage 2 Base and Stage 2 Turn
paragraphs: Before we ever upgrade ASX from WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT to an active momentum buy, the tape must clear three sequential hurdles. First, the $33.25–$35.75 support shelf—anchored by Pivot S1 ($35.21) and the rising 200-day SMA ($34.14)—must hold on any retest without a high-volume break below $31.75. Second, the 4-hour chart must flip positive: price needs to close decisively above the 4H 20-EMA ($36.41) and push 4H RSI back above 50. Third, weekly institutional sponsorship must return by reclaiming the 30-week SMA ($38.19) and 10-week EMA ($38.45) on >=1.3x average volume. Until those three boxes are checked, options spreads lack edge (1.21:1 R:R on the $35/$37.50 call spread) and cash stays patient.

Let's also explain the options math in plain beginner dollars so you know why we stamped NO_OPTIONS_EDGE. If you buy the $35/$37.50 bull call spread on ASX, you pay $1.13 per share—or $113 per contract—up front. That $113 is your maximum possible loss if ASX finishes below $35.00 at expiration. To break even, ASX must close above $36.13 ($35.00 strike plus the $1.13 debit). Even if ASX rallies cleanly above $37.50 by expiration, your maximum profit is capped at the $2.25 spread width minus your $1.13 cost, or $1.37 per share ($137 per contract). Risking $113 to make $137 is a 1.21-to-1 reward-to-risk ratio—below our desk's 1.25-to-1 minimum threshold—especially on a stock trapped beneath its 4-hour 20-EMA in a Stage 3 downtrend. Standing aside on options is pure capital preservation.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Fundamental conviction tells you WHAT to own; technical structure tells you WHEN to deploy new cash. Buying a 2.92-beta semiconductor ADR in Stage 3 below its 50-day and 30-week moving averages during a market correction is how good companies turn into painful 15% drawdowns before they ever base.
